title: The Keeper's Daughter
text: Nell had lived in the lighthouse for eleven years, and in all that time she had never once slept through a storm. Her father said this was because she had been born during one, as though the weather had marked her as its own on the very first night of her life.

Tonight the wind came in long, shuddering pushes that made the iron staircase hum. Nell counted the gaps between them the way other children counted sheep. Her father was above her in the lamp room, and she could hear the slow scrape of his boots as he walked his circle around the great glass eye of the light.

At half past two the scraping stopped. Nell sat up. She waited for it to begin again, and when it did not, she was already halfway up the stairs before she had decided to move at all. Her candle went out on the third turn, but she did not need it. She knew the number of steps better than she knew her own age.
She found him at the top, kneeling beside the mechanism with his sleeves pushed back, and the relief that flooded through her was so sudden that it came out as anger. 'You stopped walking,' she said.
'The gear's slipping,' he answered, without looking up. 'Fetch the small oil can, Nell. Quickly now.' And because there was a ship somewhere out in all that black water, she went.

title: Saturday at the Market
text: Otis did not like Saturdays, and he liked market days least of all. It was not the crowds, exactly, nor the smell of frying onions that clung to his jumper for days afterwards. It was that his grandmother expected him to be useful, and being useful meant standing behind the vegetable stall shouting prices at strangers.
'Louder,' she said, without turning round. 'A voice like that will lose us the day.'
Otis tried again. The words came out thin and apologetic, and a woman inspecting the parsnips looked up, smiled kindly, and put them back down.

His grandmother sighed the particular sigh she kept for him. Then she did something unexpected: she came and stood beside him, put one hand flat on the trestle table, and said nothing at all for a full minute. When the next customer approached, she waited. Otis, unable to bear the silence, spoke first — and this time his voice carried right across the square.
'There,' said his grandmother, moving away again. 'You had it all along. You were simply waiting for me to do it for you.'
